analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve any major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House committee vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal agencies can issue binding rules — on clean air, workplace safety, food safety, banking — and those rules take effect on their own, subject only to lawsuits and later congressional disapproval. The REINS Act would flip that: any rule the government classifies as "major" (roughly, one with $100 million or more in annual economic impact, a major increase in consumer or industry costs, or significant effects on competition, jobs, or investment) would have no force unless both chambers of Congress pass a joint resolution approving it, signed by the president, within 70 legislative days. If Congress does nothing, the rule dies. Rules that fall below that threshold would take effect unless Congress affirmatively votes them down. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be companies and industries subject to major federal regulations: any costly new rule would need an affirmative vote of both chambers and the president's signature to take effect, and in a divided Congress most such rules would simply lapse. Consumers and workers would keep the theoretical benefit of congressional accountability, but the practical effect would be that new health, safety, environmental, and financial rules rarely took effect. The bill also carves out monetary policy rules from review entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing costly federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Gives regulated industries a procedural veto over any agency rule that costs $100 million or more or raises consumer prices, since a rule takes effect only if both chambers pass, and the president signs, a resolution approving it.

Requires agencies to publish the data, studies, and cost-benefit analyses behind each rule and to report on each major rule to Congress — transparency provisions that supporters of all stripes generally back.
Creates expedited, amendment-proof floor procedures so approval or disapproval resolutions must actually get a vote in each chamber.

analysis.who_pays: The cost of a pass would fall on people who rely on federal regulatory protections — air and water quality, product safety, workplace safety, financial rules — since major rules in those areas would generally die without Congress ever voting, while politically connected industries could lobby against each rule's approval rather than face it as settled law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and workers relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: Because major rules would take effect only if Congress affirmatively approves them, and a single chamber can stop approval, any rule opposed by whichever party controls one chamber would die — a widely used tool to block consumer, workplace, and environmental protections from ever taking effect.

Congress historically passes very few laws; requiring it to act on every major rule (often 60-90 per year) would realistically mean most simply never take effect, leaving the underlying statutory protections that Congress already enacted unenforced.
The bill exempts monetary policy rules, and narrowly carves out agency-management and certain procedural rules, so some significant government actions would still escape the vote requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is accountability: unelected agencies issue rules with the force of law worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and making Congress vote on the biggest ones sounds like democratic control [S3]. The drawback is that a do-nothing Congress becomes a do-nothing regulator — the default is that major rules die, so whatever guardrails laws like the Clean Air Act promise citizens depend on a Congress functioning well enough to affirmatively approve each rule [S2][S3]. Anyone who believes agencies write rules that large industries want blocked will see this as handing those industries a veto, with almost no realistic prospect that a divided Congress approves 100+ major rules a year.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to three committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2023 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Kat Cammack introduced the REINS Act in the House on March 10, 2021, with 126 cosponsors, all Republicans.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary, Rules, and Budget Committees on the day it was introduced.
On May 18, 2021, the House Judiciary Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and no further action was taken.
No committee reported the bill, the House never voted on it, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Groups that benefit from existing federal regulations kept them in force; regulated industries gained nothing from this Congress, since the bill died.

for.name: Business and industry groups
for.what_they_did: Longstanding outside backers of the REINS Act concept, which they have lobbied for across multiple Congresses; they do not appear in the record for this bill.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda in this Congress and never brought the bill to the floor; as the majority, they also controlled committee scheduling, and the bill never received a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 126 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill stalled in a House controlled by Democrats; no Democrat cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Regulated industries generally (energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, agriculture)
industries.note: Any rule costing $100 million a year or raising consumer prices — the categories where industry opposition to regulation is most concentrated — would need an affirmative act of Congress to take effect, effectively handing those industries a veto through their allies in one chamber. Ordinary enforcement of health, safety, environmental, and financial rules would become far harder.
Agencies would lose their ability to put major rules into effect on their own authority; rules would sit until Congress acted, and would die automatically after 70 legislative days without approval.
